flawed_step: The inference that a unique minimum cut forces a unique maximum flow is unjustified. Saturating the unique minimum cut need not determine how flow is routed afterward.
counterexample: Let V={s,u,v,t} and let the only arcs be s->u, s->v, u->t, v->t, u->v, with respective capacities 1,1,2,2,1. The four s-t cuts have capacities: cap({s})=2; cap({s,u})=1+2+1=4; cap({s,v})=1+2=3; cap({s,u,v})=2+2=4. Thus {s} is the unique minimum cut. Two distinct flows are f1=(1,1,1,1,0) and f2=(1,1,0,2,1), with coordinates ordered as (s->u,s->v,u->t,v->t,u->v). Both obey all capacities and conservation: for f1, u and v each receive and send 1; for f2, u receives 1 and sends 1 to v, while v receives 2 total and sends 2. Both have value 2. Since the cut {s} has capacity 2, no flow can have value greater than 2, so both are maximum flows. They differ on three arcs.
assessment_summary: A four-vertex network can have a unique minimum cut but multiple maximum flows because flow downstream of the bottleneck can be routed in more than one way. The explicit network above disproves the statement.
